summary:
We developed the **Artemis Resource Navigator**, an interactive decision-support platform designed for lunar exploration and base planning under NASA’s Artemis program. Instead of acting as a static lunar map, the platform guides mission planners through a complete workflow—from identifying potential water-ice targets near Shackleton Crater to planning safe rover paths, running 3D mission simulations, and generating technical reports.

The platform addresses the challenge of fragmented and uncertain lunar planning data by integrating archived NASA datasets (such as LOLA, Diviner, LAMP, and M³) into a single system. Every data layer clearly labels its source, resolution, and uncertainty, distinguishing between direct measurements, derived proxies, and model estimates. Using a customizable Mining Viability Index (0–100) and a constraint-based route optimizer, planners can balance energy consumption, slope safety, and scientific return in real time.

This tool is important because safe, energy-efficient resource extraction is critical for establishing a sustainable human presence on the Moon. By providing transparent, physics-informed mission planning, the Artemis Resource Navigator helps reduce operational risks and supports data-driven decision-making for future lunar missions.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

The Artemis Resource Navigator is a native Android decision-support application built in Kotlin that transforms raw lunar orbital datasets into an end-to-end mission planning workflow under NASA’s Artemis program. Using a primary mission showcase near Shackleton Crater at the lunar south pole, the app guides planners step-by-step from scientific observation to rover execution:

  1. Transparent Multi-Layer Orbital Analysis:

    • The app integrates archived datasets from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Planetary Data System (PDS). Every map layer explicitly displays its source, spatial resolution, units, and margin of uncertainty.
      • Measured Observations: High-resolution LOLA polar elevation data (~5 meters/pixel) for mapping surface height and slope angles, alongside Diviner radiometer data for identifying extreme thermal cold traps.
      • Derived Proxies: LAMP ultraviolet albedo readings to detect potential surface frost, and LP-NS neutron spectrometer readings to detect subsurface hydrogen enrichment.
      • Model Estimates: M³ spectral mineral indicators (titanium dioxide, iron) alongside modeled estimates for ilmenite and helium-3 based on documented geological assumptions.
    • A dedicated Sources and Methodology screen allows planners to audit the exact dataset, acquisition date, and scientific formulas behind every metric.
    • Candidate extraction zones are evaluated using a transparent 0–100 relative suitability score rather than a misleading percentage probability of mining success.
    • The MVI algorithm aggregates weighted engineering variables—including terrain slope safety, thermal material stress in permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), overburden extraction depth, and Earth/relay communications line-of-sight. Users can adjust these weighting sliders in real time to observe how shifting mission priorities re-orders top targets on the leaderboard.
    • The pathfinding engine calculates rover trajectories that balance energy expenditure, hazard avoidance, and scientific return.
    • In the Shackleton Crater case study, the app contrasts a 9.2 km Direct Baseline Route—which takes the shortest path but crosses steep crater walls that exceed mechanical limits and rapidly deplete power—against a 14.8 km Optimized Safe Route that adheres to an 18° maximum slope limit and preserves a 25% return battery reserve on a 35 kWh rover battery.
    • The underlying energy model dynamically computes power draw across driving, active thermal heating, communications, rotary drilling, and sample processing. Adjusting any constraint (such as tightening the slope threshold) triggers an immediate route recalculation and energy forecast update.
    • Once a path is finalized, users execute a real-time 3D Mission Simulation at 1x, 2x, or 5x playback speeds. Live telemetry tracks rover coordinates, battery state of charge (SoC), subsystem power draw, and projected water-ice yield—explicitly labeled as simulated scenario outputs based on assumed regolith ice concentrations and excavation rates.
    • Upon mission completion, the app compiles all orbital inputs, route trade-off metrics, and simulation logs into a structured technical report ready for engineering review.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Eliminating Data Ambiguity: By visually and mathematically separating direct sensor measurements from indirect proxies and theoretical models, mission planners avoid treating subsurface hydrogen spikes as guaranteed, recoverable water-ice reserves.
  • De-Risking Surface Operations: Simulating thermal overhead, steep crater gradients, and battery reserves prior to deployment helps prevent catastrophic rover immobilization or power loss in harsh polar environments.
  • Accelerating Artemis & ISRU Planning: By consolidating fragmented planetary science archives and complex pathfinding into an accessible, repeatable workflow, the platform supports rapid feasibility studies for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) and sustainable lunar base siting.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software

  • Programming Language: Kotlin (utilizing Kotlin Coroutines and Flow for asynchronous spatial calculations, state management, and smooth real-time UI updates).
    • Custom Kotlin pathfinding and constraint-satisfaction algorithms (A*/Dijkstra variants weighted by slope cost and energy consumption).
    • Real-time physics and subsystem energy-budget calculators modeling battery discharge, thermal heating loads, and excavation rates.
    • Interactive 2D elevation/heatmap overlays and a custom 3D rendering viewport for real-time rover trajectory and telemetry playback.
  • Data Handling: Local structured parsing and caching of processed NASA LRO/PDS geospatial grids (LOLA, Diviner, LAMP, LP-NS, M³) for offline field and classroom usability.

Creativity & Key Engineering Considerations

  • Creative Approach: Rather than building another passive desktop GIS map viewer or focusing on superficial visual effects, we engineered a unified "observation-to-operation" mobile sandbox. Bringing multi-dataset planetary analysis, live multi-criteria decision weighting, and 3D rover telemetry together on Android allows students, researchers, and planners to test "what-if" engineering trade-offs in seconds.
    • Lunar Physical Realism: Every formula reflects real lunar constraints—accounting for the Moon’s near-vacuum environment, extreme cryogenic temperatures in shadowed craters, cold-induced mechanical stress, and feasible mobility architectures (prioritizing future support for ballistic robotic hoppers rather than propeller drones, which cannot generate lift in a vacuum).
    • Engineering Honesty & Uncertainty: We prioritized scientific integrity over oversimplified answers—framing the MVI strictly as a relative ranking under stated assumptions and designing our roadmap around formal uncertainty propagation, deeper thermal-power coupling, and physical terrestrial analog validation.
